meta.title: Who really said "A sex symbol is a heavy load to carry when one is tired, hurt and bewildered"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Marilyn Monroe. The line belongs to Clara Bow, the 1920s “It Girl,” who said it of Monroe after her 1962 death — then it boomeranged back onto Monroe.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'A sex symbol is a heavy load to carry when one is tired, hurt and bewildered'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Marilyn Monroe. It was Clara Bow, the original “It Girl,” reflecting on Monroe’s death in 1962. Here’s the sourced story.

answer.label: Not Marilyn Monroe — actually Clara Bow
answer.sourceLine: The line was spoken by Clara Bow — the 1920s “It Girl” and Hollywood’s first great sex symbol — reflecting on Marilyn Monroe’s death in August 1962. Monroe herself did make a famous remark about being a sex symbol in her final Life interview, but it was a different one (“a sex symbol becomes a thing… I just hate to be a thing”). Over the decades Bow’s poignant sentence was quietly re-pinned onto the very star it was about.

source.heading: The real source
source.excerpt: A sex symbol is a heavy load to carry when one is tired, hurt, and bewildered.
trail: Wikiquote lists the line in its Marilyn Monroe “Misattributed” section and notes it “was actually said by Clara Bow.”

The reference entry Encyclopedia.com’s Clara Bow biography carries the exact wording: “Bow herself identified with Marilyn Monroe, saying of her death, ‘A sex symbol is a heavy load to carry when one is tired, hurt, and bewildered.’”
Monroe’s genuine sex-symbol line came from her 1962 Life interview with Richard Meryman — a different sentence, as Quote Investigator documents.
source.excerptNote: Clara Bow’s words on the death of Marilyn Monroe, with whom she strongly identified. A fuller circulating variant reads “Being a sex symbol is a heavy load to carry, especially when one is very tired, hurt and bewildered.”
source.rightsNote: This is a spoken remark by Clara Bow from around August 1962; it survives through later biographies and reference entries rather than a single pinned first-publication, so no clean copyright date can be asserted. It is plainly a 20th-century utterance, not a pre-1931 work, so it is not public domain; the exact first print appearance is undetermined.

author.name: Clara Bow
author.kicker: The real voice behind the line
author.heading: Clara Bow
author.bio: Clara Bow was the breakout sex symbol of the 1920s, whose turn as a magnetic shopgirl in the 1927 film It made her “The It Girl” and one of the biggest stars of the silent era. Chewed up by fame, scandal and studio pressure, she retired young and lived reclusively for decades. When Marilyn Monroe — a later star endlessly compared to her — died in 1962, Bow spoke about the private cost of being a public sex symbol, having carried that weight herself.

misattribution.heading: How it landed on Marilyn Monroe
misattribution.intro: This is a boomerang quote: a line said about Marilyn Monroe by an earlier sex symbol eventually got reassigned to Monroe herself — a natural mix-up, since both the subject and the speaker were famous for the very burden the sentence describes.

items.scope: All over social media, quote sites and merchandise
items.why: Databases like BrainyQuote and Quotefancy print it under Monroe’s name with no source, and Wikiquote files it as misattributed.
Bow, who identified strongly with Monroe, said it of Monroe’s death; the exact wording appears in Encyclopedia.com’s Bow entry.

misattribution.truthLine: The words are Clara Bow’s, spoken about Marilyn Monroe in 1962 — not Monroe’s own; Monroe’s real sex-symbol line was the separate “a sex symbol becomes a thing” from her final Life interview.

context.heading: Why the mix-up makes sense
lead: Clara Bow and Marilyn Monroe were the same archetype a generation apart — the era-defining screen sex symbol whose private self was crushed by the public one. Bow burned out under exactly the scrutiny she describes, retreating from Hollywood while still young.

So when Bow reacted to Monroe’s 1962 death with this sentence, she was speaking as someone who had carried the identical load. Detached from that context and passed around online, the empathy of one sex symbol for another was easily misread as Monroe describing herself.
context.pull: A line said in sympathy for Monroe became a line spoken as Monroe.
